summary: Published as a historical record of version 3.0 of the Secure Sockets Layer protocol, which provides privacy and integrity for client-server communication and was the basis for TLS. It is historic, and SSL 3.0 should not be used today.

plainLanguage.summary: SSL 3.0 is the protocol that put encryption underneath ordinary web traffic. RFC 6101 republishes it as a stable reference, since the original was never formally published. It describes two layers: a record layer that wraps, encrypts and checks each piece of data, and a handshake that agrees the algorithms, proves the server's identity and derives the keys.

subtitle: A historical record of the protocol that gave the web its encrypted connections, and the basis for TLS.

tldr.problem: Applications running over TCP needed a way to keep their traffic private, to check that the peer was who it claimed to be, and to detect damage or tampering, without changing the application protocol itself.
tldr.mechanism: SSL adds a record layer that encrypts and checks every piece of data, and a handshake that agrees the algorithms, proves the server's identity and derives the session keys.
tldr.outcome: SSL 3.0 became the basis for TLS, but it was never published by the IETF, so RFC 6101 was written in 2011 to give the last version of it a stable reference. It is Historic and should not be used.

today: RFC 6101 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in August 2011 as a historical record of SSL 3.0, the protocol the RFC says was the basis for TLS. Its own security analysis warns that the system is only as strong as its weakest key exchange and authentication algorithm, and that short public keys, 40-bit bulk encryption keys and anonymous servers should be used with great caution.

sections.title: What SSL Sets Out to Provide
sections.content:
The primary goal of the SSL protocol is to provide privacy and reliability between two communicating applications. It is built in two layers. At the lowest level, on top of a reliable transport protocol such as TCP, sits the SSL record protocol, which encapsulates higher level protocols. One of the protocols it carries is the SSL handshake, which lets the client and server authenticate each other and agree an encryption algorithm and cryptographic keys before the application protocol sends or receives its first byte of data. A useful property of SSL is that it does not depend on the application protocol: a higher level protocol can sit on top of it transparently.

The connection security it provides has three basic properties. The connection is private: after an initial handshake defines a secret key, symmetric cryptography such as DES, 3DES or RC4 is used for the data itself. The peer's identity can be authenticated with asymmetric, or public key, cryptography such as RSA or DSS. And the connection is reliable, because message transport includes an integrity check computed as a keyed Message Authentication Code, using secure hash functions such as SHA or MD5.

The RFC also explains why it exists at all. SSL 3.0 was widely implemented and was a pioneer in secure communications protocols, and the basis for Transport Layer Security, but it was never formally published by the IETF, only in several expired Internet-Drafts, so it could not be easily referenced. RFC 6101 therefore describes what is known as the last published version of SSL 3.0, the version of 18 November 1996, with only trivial editorial changes and an added security section. Portions that no longer apply were left out, including the patent statement, the reserved ports assignment and the note about who registers cipher suites.
sections.plainLanguage: SSL gave any TCP program three things without changing the program: a private channel, a way to check who is on the other end, and a way to notice if the data was altered. This RFC exists so that the original text of the protocol has a citable home.

sections.title: The Record Layer
sections.content:
The record layer takes whatever the higher layers hand it, in blocks of arbitrary size, and fragments it into records of 2^14 bytes or less. It does not preserve the boundaries between the client's messages, so several messages of the same type may end up in one record. Each record carries a type saying which higher level protocol should handle it, the protocol version, a length, and the fragment itself. There are four types: change cipher spec, alert, handshake and application data. Data of different types may be interleaved, and application data generally has lower precedence for transmission.

All records are compressed with the algorithm in the current session state. There is always an active compression algorithm, but at first it is the null method. Compression must be lossless and may not make the content longer by more than 1024 bytes, and a fragment that would decompress to more than 2^14 bytes should raise a fatal decompression failure alert.

All records are also protected with the encryption and MAC algorithms in the current CipherSpec. There is always an active CipherSpec, but at first it is SSL_NULL_WITH_NULL_NULL, which gives no security at all. Once the handshake is complete the two parties hold shared secrets used to encrypt records and compute MACs over them. Each transmission carries a sequence number, so missing, altered or extra messages can be detected. The encrypted record may be at most 2^14 + 2048 bytes.

The MAC is computed before encryption, over the record's type, length and fragment together with the sequence number and the write secret, using a padding byte of 0x36 repeated 48 times for MD5 or 40 times for SHA, and a second padding byte of 0x5c. The stream cipher then encrypts the whole block, MAC included. With a block cipher in CBC mode the record is padded to a multiple of the block length, and the initialisation vector for the first record comes from the handshake; for later records it is the last ciphertext block of the previous record.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything the application sends is cut into pieces of at most 16 kilobytes. Each piece gets a small header saying what it is, is compressed, is encrypted and carries a check value so that missing or altered pieces are noticed.

sections.title: The Handshake
sections.content:
When a client and server first start talking, they agree a protocol version, choose cryptographic algorithms, optionally authenticate each other and use public key techniques to generate shared secrets. The client sends a client hello, and the server must answer with a server hello or the connection fails. The two hello messages fix the protocol version, the session identifier, the cipher suite and the compression method, and they exchange two random values, ClientHello.random and ServerHello.random. Each random value is four bytes of the sender's clock followed by 28 bytes from a secure random number generator; the RFC notes that the basic protocol does not require the clock to be right.

The server then sends its certificate if it is to be authenticated, and may send a server key exchange message if one is needed, for example when it has no certificate or when its certificate is for signing only. If the server is authenticated it may ask the client for a certificate. The server hello done message ends this phase, and the client replies with its own certificate or a no-certificate alert, then the client key exchange message, and then a certificate verify message if the certificate it sent had signing ability.

The client then sends a change cipher spec message and copies the pending CipherSpec into the current one, and sends the finished message under the new algorithms and keys. The server answers with its own change cipher spec and finished message, and the handshake is over. The client hello carries the list of cipher suites the client supports in order of preference, and the server picks one or returns a handshake failure alert and closes the connection. The list of compression methods is offered the same way, and every implementation must support the null method.

Two messages carry the key agreement itself. A server key exchange message holds either the modulus and exponent of a temporary RSA key or the prime, generator and public value for Diffie-Hellman, together with a signature over a hash of those parameters. A client key exchange message holds, for RSA, a 48-byte premaster secret encrypted under the server's public key, made up of the client's version number and 46 random bytes; the client version is there to detect version rollback attacks. With Diffie-Hellman the message carries the client's public value, unless it was already in its certificate.

The finished message is always sent right after a change cipher spec message and is the first thing protected with the new algorithms. It carries MD5 and SHA hashes over all the handshake messages, the master secret and a marker saying who sent it. It is a fatal error if a finished message is not preceded by a change cipher spec message at the right point.

A previous session can be resumed instead. The client sends a client hello naming the session it wants to reuse, and if the server finds it in its session cache and is willing to re-establish the connection under that session state, it answers with a server hello carrying the same session identifier. Both sides then send change cipher spec and go straight to the finished messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The opening exchange is a fixed sequence of messages. The client says what it can do, the server picks, proves who it is, and the two sides agree a secret that nobody watching can work out. Each side then proves it computed the same secret by sending a hash of everything said so far.

sections.title: From Pre-Master Secret to Session Keys
sections.content:
Whichever key exchange was used, the same formula turns the pre-master secret into the master secret: three MD5 hashes, each over the pre-master secret and a SHA hash of a different marker string, the pre-master secret and the two random values from the hello messages. The pre-master secret should be erased from memory once the master secret has been computed.

With RSA the client generates the 48-byte pre-master secret, encrypts it under the server's public key and sends it; the server decrypts it with its private key. RSA signatures use PKCS number 1 block type 1 and public key encryption uses PKCS number 1 block type 2. With Diffie-Hellman an ordinary computation is performed and the negotiated key is used directly as the pre-master secret.

The master secret is a 48-byte quantity known only to the two parties, and the keys and MAC secrets for the session are derived from it. The master secret is hashed into a key block, again with the same three MD5 and SHA construction, until enough output has been produced. The key block is then split in order into a client write MAC secret, a server write MAC secret, a client write key, a server write key, a client write IV and a server write IV, and any leftover material is discarded. The master secret supplies the entropy, while the two random values provide unencrypted salt material and initialisation vectors for exportable ciphers. For those, the write keys are salted once more with MD5 over the key and the two random values.

The RFC gives a worked example. The suite SSL_RSA_EXPORT_WITH_RC2_CBC_40_MD5 needs five random bytes for each of the two encryption keys and 16 bytes for each of the MAC keys, 42 bytes in all. MD5 produces 16 bytes per call, so three calls are needed, giving a 48-byte key block that is then split and salted.
sections.plainLanguage: The value agreed during the handshake is not used to encrypt anything directly. Both sides mix it with the random values they exchanged to produce a master secret, and then split that master secret into the separate keys each side needs to encrypt and to check what it sends.

sections.title: Alerts and Closing the Connection
sections.content:
The change cipher spec protocol exists to signal a change in the ciphering strategy. It is a single message, a one-byte value, encrypted and compressed under the current CipherSpec rather than the pending one. Both sides send it, to tell the other that the records after it will be protected under the newly negotiated CipherSpec and keys. On receipt the receiver copies its read pending state into its read current state. The client sends it after the key exchange and any certificate verify message, and the server after it has successfully processed the client's key exchange message. An unexpected change cipher spec message should raise an unexpected message alert.

The alert protocol conveys the severity of a message and a description of it. An alert at the fatal level ends the connection immediately. Other connections belonging to the same session may continue, but the session identifier must be invalidated so that the failed session cannot be used to open new connections. Alerts are encrypted and compressed according to the current connection state.

Alerts have two levels, warning and fatal, and a list of descriptions: close notify, unexpected message, bad record MAC, decompression failure, handshake failure, no certificate, bad certificate, unsupported certificate, certificate revoked, certificate expired, certificate unknown and illegal parameter. A connection is closed by sending a close notify alert, so that each side knows the other has finished sending and that no data is lost in the shutdown.
sections.plainLanguage: Either side can send a short warning or a fatal error. A fatal error closes the connection at once and makes the session unusable for new connections, so that a later attempt cannot reuse keys from a session that failed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 7 points to Appendix F for the security analysis, and the appendix is where the RFC's own warnings sit. The final notes there are blunt: for SSL to provide a secure connection, the client and server systems, keys and applications must all be secure, and the implementation must be free of security errors. The system is only as strong as the weakest key exchange and authentication algorithm it supports, and only trustworthy cryptographic functions should be used. Short public keys, 40-bit bulk encryption keys and anonymous servers should be used with great caution. Implementations and users must be careful about which certificates and certificate authorities they accept, because a dishonest certificate authority can do tremendous damage.

The appendix also analyses two attacks on the handshake. An attacker may try to make a version 3.0 capable client and server fall back to version 2.0; the RFC explains the padding trick that lets a version 3.0 server detect this, and notes that it does not help against an attacker able to brute force the key. An attacker who changes a handshake message to influence the algorithm choice is caught by the finished messages, because the two sides compute different hashes and will not accept each other's finished message, and without the master secret the attacker cannot repair them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document's own analysis says the whole scheme is only as good as its weakest algorithm and its correct implementation. It singles out short keys, 40-bit encryption keys and servers that do not present a certificate as the things to be most careful about.

messages.label: ClientHello
messages.note: Offers the cipher suites and compression methods, a session identifier and 32 bytes of randomness.

messages.label: ServerHello
messages.note: Chooses the cipher suite and compression method and supplies the server's own random value.

messages.label: Certificate
messages.note: Sent when the server is to be authenticated.

messages.label: ServerKeyExchange
messages.note: Sent when one is needed, with the key exchange parameters and a signature over them.

messages.label: CertificateRequest
messages.note: Optional. Asks the client for a certificate.

messages.label: ServerHelloDone
messages.note: Ends the server's part of the handshake.

messages.label: Certificate
messages.note: Sent only if the server asked for one.

messages.label: ClientKeyExchange
messages.note: Carries the encrypted premaster secret, or the client's Diffie-Hellman public value.

messages.label: CertificateVerify
messages.note: Sent only if the client certificate had signing ability.

messages.label: ChangeCipherSpec
messages.note: The records after this use the newly negotiated keys.

messages.label: Finished
messages.note: The first message protected with the new keys. It proves both sides computed the same secrets.

messages.label: Finished
messages.note: The server's proof that it computed the same secrets.

messages.label: Application Data
messages.note: The application's own traffic, now encrypted and checked.

viz.caption: THE FOUR SSL RECORD CONTENT TYPES

items.label: change_cipher_spec
items.desc: Signals that the records after it are protected under the newly negotiated cipher suite.

items.label: alert
items.desc: Carries a severity and a description, such as a warning or a fatal error.

items.label: handshake
items.desc: Carries the negotiation messages that set up the secure session.

items.label: application_data
items.desc: Carries the application's own data, encrypted and checked.
